text: Getting Started with WFScript Build an application, not just a script. WFScript combines a visual Panel Designer, a JavaScript runtime, native instrumentation, charts, and a Test Executive in one Windows application. You arrange the interface, give its controls meaningful IDs, and connect user actions to JavaScript procedures. When the Panel runs, those same components become an operator interface. The DSP Studio is a bundled, simulation-only example. It demonstrates interactive controls, native plots, and reusable JavaScript modules without requiring hardware. This guide follows the shortest useful path: open an example, change it, build a small Panel from scratch, work with shared data, then explore instrumentation and automated testing. You do not need to connect an Analog Discovery 3 or a Rigol instrument to complete the first exercises. 1. A map of the workspace WFScript has a few distinct working areas. The Panel Designer is where you arrange Pages and widgets; Script Editor is where you write JavaScript; device-specific tools expose the instrument APIs; and the Test Sequence Editor lets you define native, reportable test steps. Area What you do there What it produces Panel Designer Add Pages, widgets, IDs, styles, events, and shared variables A visual application Script Editor Write functions, callbacks, processing code and module calls Application behavior Properties / Events Configure the selected widget and connect events to named handlers Saved, inspectable event bindings Properties / Panel Data Define typed values shared across Pages State and value bindings Test Sequence Editor Configure Setup, Main, Cleanup, limits, sweeps, branching and reports A project-owned automated test Operator View Use the Panel as an application, without developer controls The working interface A Panel is the complete project, normally saved as a .wfpanel file. A Panel can contain multiple Pages, controls, JavaScript, embedded libraries, data definitions, and a Test Executive. It is not just a screenshot of a UI or a link to an external script. 2. Open your first example From Panel Designer , choose Examples and open Getting Started . It has a Guide Page and an Events Tutorial Page. Read the Guide Page, then switch to Events Tutorial . In Design mode, select the CLICK ME button, open Properties → Events , and inspect its clicked binding. The saved handler is onTourButtonClicked() . Use Go to Handler to jump to the implementation in the script editor. This illustrates an important rule: a widget's event binding belongs to the Panel project; JavaScript supplies the named function that runs when the event fires. Choose Run Panel , click the tutorial button twice, and watch the count change. Then use Stop / Design , change a line in the handler, and run again. A developer can iterate on a Panel without rebuilding the C++ application. The bundled example is the authority for the exact handler body. Do not replace its counter code with the shorter snippets in an introduction unless you intend to change its behavior. 3. Understand Design and Run Design mode is for editing layout and properties. Selecting a widget opens its configuration instead of performing the operator action. Run mode starts the Panel's JavaScript runtime and makes those controls operational. A focused operator view gives the application more space, hiding most editing tools. F11 or Esc restores the development layout without necessarily stopping the active Panel. Stop / Design ends the Panel runtime and returns it to editing mode. That difference is useful when debugging: you can inspect live data without treating every change of view as a new run. Save a copy of examples under your own .wfpanel filename before making extensive changes. Run-time values are not always the saved design-time defaults; Panel Data initial values, for example, belong to the project, while its live values belong to the current execution. 4. text: WFScript User Guide Visual application development, JavaScript, data acquisition, and automated testing WFScript is a Windows Qt application for building interactive instrument and test software. A Panel is both the application project and the operator interface: it holds Pages, widgets, designer-managed events, JavaScript, optional libraries, named Panel Data, and an optional native Test Executive. This guide is organized around common jobs rather than the order in which the software's features were developed. Who this is for. Developers, lab engineers, researchers, technicians and technically curious people who want to write software close to their measurements and equipment. Prior JavaScript experience helps, but the first chapters do not assume it. You can complete the initial workflows without physical instrumentation. Version basis. RC1.5.14.10.8, source-verified and built with Qt 6.9.2 MinGW 64-bit on Windows; 116/116 registered native CTests passed. Public WFScript v0.1 remains a separate release. This guide distinguishes software-tested, simulated and physically verified capabilities. Browse chapters 1: How WFScript fits together 2: Panels, Pages and the design workflow 3: Widgets, styling and interaction 4: JavaScript, callbacks and modules 5: Shared Panel Data and computed values 6: Charts and measurements 7: Analog Discovery 3 instrumentation 8: Digital timing, I/O and protocols 9: Serial, TCP and UDP communications 10: Files, SQLite and native binary data 11: The native Test Executive 12: Sweeps, loops and conditional execution 13: Operator input and manual steps 14: Reports, measurements and history 15: External Rigol instruments and SCPI Panels 16: Building complete applications 17: Troubleshooting without guessing 18: Testing, validation and publication Each chapter is a standalone page so you can return directly to the operation you need.

text: Chapter 1 — How WFScript fits together A typical WFScript application has four layers. The Panel Designer stores the visual structure; the JavaScript runtime handles actions and calculations; native bridges perform Qt, file, communication and instrument operations; and the optional Test Executive schedules verifiable steps and creates reports. Most simple applications use just the first two. A dashboard may add Panel Data and charts. An automated measurement application may use all four. Layer Responsible for Generally avoid putting here Panel/Page Layout, widget properties, visual event bindings, named variables Instrument transaction sequences Main Panel script Initialization, UI event handlers, small application coordination Hundreds of repetitive test procedures Embedded modules Reusable signal processing, drivers and operations Hidden UI changes that make behavior hard to trace Native Test Executive Step state, timing, expansion, limits, Cleanup and report lifecycle Ad-hoc scheduling through long blocking JavaScript loops A Panel can have many Pages but shares one active script environment during a run. When designing multi-page interfaces, use Pages to organize operator tasks rather than starting separate processes for each Page. A multi-page Panel is still one program. What the runtime is—and isn't Panel scripts run in Qt QJSEngine , not Node.js or a browser. There is no implied browser DOM, fetch() , Node require() or Node filesystem module. WFScript supplies its own native services, such as Serial , TCP , UDP , FileIO , Database , Binary , Tool , Data and plots when available in the relevant context. Embedded .mjs libraries use the application's supported module mechanism. The long-lived Panel script worker processes callbacks and Qt-backed events. A blocking JavaScript loop or wait() delays other work on that worker. Keep event handlers finite; schedule later actions with a timer or a bridge callback when possible. When to use the standalone Script Editor Use it for concise experiments, API exploration and direct instrument exercises. Use a Panel when you want persistent controls, an operator interface, named shared data, communication sessions, or a visual test sequence. These are different contexts, and not every Panel-only global is available to standalone scripts. Next chapter →

text: Chapter 2 — Panels, Pages and the design workflow Start a Panel with New Panel , or open a bundled example. The left Toolbox groups widgets into control, display, chart, communication, education and test categories. The center canvas contains the Page; the right-hand pane shows Properties, Events and Panel Data. Give each Page a name that describes the operator's task: Overview , Measurements , Diagnostics , Report . Page navigation is part of the application; it is not a separate browser route. You can create and resize Pages, customize their appearance, and choose a theme-following or fixed-dark presentation where supported. Naming a good Panel The Panel filename should identify the application, not just the equipment. For example, DC_Power_Qualification.wfpanel is more informative than Test1.wfpanel . Use visible captions for the operator and stable widget IDs for code. A button could display START TEST while retaining the code ID startTestButton . When saving, remember that Save to Panel in the Test Sequence Editor only commits that editor's work to the in-memory Panel project. It does not replace the separate Save/Export step that writes the .wfpanel file to disk. Choosing an example The built-in examples are working projects, not slides. Getting Started demonstrates saved events; Panel Data Lab demonstrates shared typed values; JavaScript DSP Studio demonstrates charts and modules; Automated Test Station demonstrates the native test framework; and AC Network Laboratory and RC Step Response Laboratory show more elaborate analysis. A fast way to understand a feature is to open the matching example in Design mode and compare three views: selected widget properties, the saved handler name, and the corresponding JavaScript function. You can then modify a small, isolated property and rerun. What belongs in an operator application Operators should see the state of the process, clear primary actions, and meaningful feedback. Avoid putting a full source listing on the operator Page. Separate infrequent setup and diagnostics from controls used in every run. Use numeric units, explicit statuses and a concise representation of failures, not a dense wall of text. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 3 — Widgets, styling and interaction A widget has a type , a stable ID , properties and (for interactive types) events. Types range from simple Buttons and Labels to Numeric Steppers, sliders, latching switches, digital displays, meters, charts, tables, image and equation widgets, communication terminals, and Test Executive result displays. An ID is the programmatic name. Keep it unique within the Panel model and avoid renaming it casually once scripts or data bindings depend on it. A caption tells the operator what the control does, and can change without changing code. The designer-managed event pattern The usual workflow is: select widget → Properties → Events → choose the event → assign a named JavaScript function → run. The saved mapping survives project save/reopen and is visible to another developer. This is preferable to hiding dozens of ui.on() subscriptions in initialization code. Manual event subscriptions remain useful for advanced cases, but don't duplicate an existing designer binding. function onApplyClicked() { const requested = Number(ui.get('setpointInput')); if (!Number.isFinite(requested)) { ui.set('statusLabel', 'Enter a valid number'); return; } ui.set('statusLabel', 'Requested: ' + requested); } This snippet updates a display only; it does not configure hardware. Connecting a setpoint to actual equipment requires additional range validation, connection readiness, output-state protection and error handling. Geometry, typography and themes Choose a small set of visual patterns: consistent control height, predictable spacing, paired label/value displays, and colors that convey meaning rather than decorate everything. If an operator must read a value across a bench, use a large digital display instead of a small editable text box. Charts should have clear titles, channel labels and units. WFScript has widget-level theme behavior and per-Panel appearance options. The completed UI should be checked in the chosen Run theme; not every QPalette color is the same in design and operator view. Test important interactions both with the focused Page and with the development panes visible. Which widget should I choose? Need Usually use Why Operator action Button or Momentary Button Clear one-shot event Persistent enable state Latching Switch or Toggle Reflects an ongoing Boolean value Setpoint Numeric Stepper Constrained numeric input Continuous adjustment Slider Direct manipulation with a visible range Measurement Digital Display or Measurement Result Readable value, optional verdict context State Status Beacon, Label or Event Log Clear status, descriptive messages Trend and waveforms Chart/Plot Time, XY, digital or spectral view Test report Measurement Table, Sequence and Results Browser Native result semantics When a widget acts as a read-only indicator, do not treat it as an operator input. For example, a status beacon is an output display; a Toggle is a better choice for a Boolean operator command. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 4 — JavaScript, callbacks and modules Write JavaScript to describe behavior, not to redraw widgets or poll every property continually. Most useful Panel scripts define a few constants, subscribe to genuinely asynchronous services, and expose named handlers for saved events. The JavaScript editor includes syntax highlighting and integrated API exploration. API documentation and autocomplete are aids, not proof that a device supports every possible setting. Validate parameter ranges and read errors back from the actual bridge. A readable startup structure var refreshTimer = 0; function onInitialize() { ui.set('statusLabel', 'Ready'); // Start services only when this Panel needs them. } function onRefreshClicked() { ui.set('statusLabel', 'Refresh requested'); } function onShutdown() { if (refreshTimer) clearInterval(refreshTimer); } The lifecycle hooks are optional and enabled in Panel properties where appropriate. Clean up timers and application sessions explicitly if you own them. The native runtime also manages certain resources as part of a normal stop, but an application's physical equipment state should never depend on a JavaScript handler being guaranteed after a sudden failure. Modules versus classic includes Use modules.load('MathTools.mjs') for a modern embedded module with named exports. Use include('Helpers.js') for a classic script where appropriate. The two are not interchangeable with Node's package loader. A Panel may embed .mjs libraries so it can open on another computer without requiring the original external source tree. var dsp = modules.load('DSPCore.mjs'); var magnitude = dsp.magnitude(samples); The example shows the call shape; DSPCore.mjs must be present in the Panel or a supported library location, and its actual export names must match the module. The bundled JavaScript DSP Studio demonstrates a source-backed module workflow. Timers are cooperative setTimeout() and setInterval() use Qt's event loop in the Panel worker, with clearTimeout() and clearInterval() for cancellation. Intervals are best-effort; do not use them as a hard real-time clock or as a substitute for sample-accurate hardware capture. var updates = 0; var timer = setInterval(function() { updates++; ui.set('counterLabel', 'Update ' + updates); }, 250); // Later: clearInterval(timer); Use Scope1 or Logic1 for hardware-timed capture, not a setInterval() that toggles a DIO output and assumes microsecond accuracy. Error handling and console output A value that looks numeric may be an overload, a disconnected measurement, or a failed query. Convert and validate explicitly. Use print() , console.warn() and console.error() where supported, then give the operator a concise status in the Panel. The Console can be filtered without erasing the original output history. For asynchronous work, the error belongs in the callback or Promise rejection. A try/catch around the code that schedules a network request cannot catch a failure that arrives later unless that failure is explicitly propagated into a Promise chain. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 5 — Shared Panel Data and computed values Panel Data is the common state model for a multi-widget Panel. It allows several Pages and controls to use the same typed values while keeping view-specific IDs separate from application state. Declare values in Properties → Panel Data . Typical types are Number, Boolean and Text, with optional choice-type constraints. The designer saves their initial values. The runtime exposes live values while the Panel runs; stopping does not automatically rewrite initial values in the project. Bind once, display many times A motor dashboard might expose Motor.TargetRPM , Motor.ActualRPM , Motor.Ready , and Motor.Mode . A target control, large digital display and gauge can each reflect one or more of those values through Value Binding. Instead of separately pushing the same speed into three widgets, a script does: Data.set('Motor.ActualRPM', 1725.0); All widgets bound to that value refresh. The value is still a simulation unless it originates from an actual instrument or sensor. Two ways to respond to change Bind a widget's saved valueChanged event to a handler when you care about an operator action. Use Data.onChange(name, callback, {immediate:true}) when you care about a shared variable regardless of which widget or script changed it. var watcher = Data.onChange('Motor.Ready', function(value) { ui.set('readinessLabel', value ? 'READY' : 'NOT READY'); }, {immediate:true}); Keep these callbacks small and avoid writing back the same value endlessly. The native bridge guards against unbounded notification feedback, but clear ownership of data is better than relying on a guard. Derived values belong in formulas Data.computed(target,dependencies,formula) creates a run-time read-only derived value from existing declared variables. Dependencies are explicit, with values supplied to the function in the listed order. Data.computed('Motor.TargetRPS', ['Motor.TargetRPM'], function(rpm) { return rpm / 60; }); A computed target must already be declared and should be bound to a read-only display. Its registration is evaluated at runtime; the formula lives in ordinary saved JavaScript. Use pure expressions—do not call Data.set() inside a computed formula. The source limits registration to 64 computed variables with 1–16 dependencies each. Why direct widget assignment can fail A widget with a Value Binding is controlled by shared data. Calling ui.set(widgetId, value) for that bound value is rejected rather than silently competing with the binding. Correct the underlying variable via Data.set(dataName, value) or change the binding in Design mode. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 6 — Charts and measurements Charting is a core application feature, not an afterthought. WFScript can display calculated values, CSV rows, digital patterns, and instrument-captured samples. Its chart subsystem supports XY/time plots, digital timing views, cursors, inspection and native high-volume sample paths. Acquisition and display are separate jobs Acquire samples with the correct device API, or construct a numerical array in JavaScript. Transform the data if needed. Then publish series to the chart. This separation makes the same plot useful whether its data came from an AD3 scope, external SCPI instrument, simulation, or file. For ordinary arrays, the plotting API includes plots.configure() and plots.setSeries() . For large buffers, review the native bulk methods and BinarySamples paths in the API Reference; passing thousands of scalar values through the script-to-Qt boundary can dominate the execution cost. plots.configure('responsePlot', { chartType: 'XY', xLabel: 'Frequency (Hz)', yLabel: 'Gain (dB)' }); plots.setSeries('responsePlot', 'Response', frequencyHz, gainDb); The ID responsePlot must belong to a compatible chart widget, and the arrays must have matching lengths. Numeric inputs should be finite. Use the appropriate chart type for XY data versus digital transitions. Read charts like instruments Make the measured unit and source visible. A trace named “Voltage” is less useful than “CH1 — input (V)”. Preserve the same series identity during updates so zoom, visibility and visual styles behave predictably. Frequency responses should communicate logarithmic/linear scale and whether the values are derived or device-computed. The bundled JavaScript DSP Studio demonstrates a signal/time graph, an FFT spectrum and a low-pass Bode-style response. Its data are synthetic; the chart techniques are equally applicable to measured data. Don't confuse calculated and instrument-provided measurements An oscilloscope may report its own Vpp, frequency and RMS measurements, while a script may compute those statistics from a transferred sample array. These can differ because of sample windows, triggering, filtering, instrument algorithms and calibration. Record the method used before comparing a result against a strict acceptance limit. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 7 — Analog Discovery 3 instrumentation WFScript includes native WaveForms SDK bindings for supported Digilent instruments, including the Analog Discovery 3. Its instrument globals use familiar names: Device , Scope1 , Wavegen1 , Supplies , StaticIO , Patterns1 , Logic1 and Protocol1 . Aliases such as Scope and Wavegen may refer to the same underlying native object rather than a separate hardware session. Start by establishing what is connected Before changing hardware state, check device availability and the model-specific capabilities. An API member being present does not mean every capability, voltage range or digital pin mode is available on every device. if (!Device.isConnected()) { print('No instrument connection available'); } else { print('Device:', Device.name); } In simulation, values are suitable for UI and algorithm demonstrations, not for validating physical accuracy. Mark simulated values clearly in both operator displays and reports. Capture a scope waveform The primary pattern is configure → arm/single → wait for completion → inspect data → release/stop. Exact object properties and ranges are listed in the Script API reference. The simplified outline below shows the sequencing without implying that the chosen sample rate is possible on every connected device. Scope1.Time.Samples.value = 4096; Scope1.Time.Rate.value = 1000000; Scope1.Channel1.enable = true; if (!Scope1.single()) throw Error(Scope1.lastError); if (!Scope1.wait()) throw Error(Scope1.lastError); const volts = Scope1.Channel1.data; Choose a suitable input range before capture. A smaller scope range may saturate when a DC supply is above the configured window; saturation is not evidence that the supply is producing the clipped voltage. Use a known test waveform, check input ratings and termination, and examine actual capture metadata. Produce a waveform Wavegen1 offers analog output capabilities including simple functions and model-supported advanced modes. Start with the output disabled, set a known shape, frequency and amplitude, then explicitly start it. Stop outputs when finished; don't rely on closing a display widget to make an electrical output safe. Wavegen1.Channel1.enable = true; Wavegen1.Channel1.Simple.Type.text = 'Sine'; Wavegen1.Channel1.Simple.Frequency.value = 1000; Wavegen1.Channel1.Simple.Amplitude.value = 1; if (!Wavegen1.run()) throw Error(Wavegen1.lastError); // Acquire a matching waveform, then stop/release the output. The example assumes a safe loopback circuit and the device's amplitude convention; inspect the device documentation and the complete bridge API before connecting a load. Power supplies are active outputs The positive and negative supplies expose staged settings, enable controls, and explicit run/config behavior. A successful request does not independently prove the terminal voltage; use scope or multimeter measurement when physical verification matters. Before a demonstration, disconnect sensitive circuits and work inside the device's safe voltage/current capabilities. A safe first hardware experiment Use a short BNC or otherwise appropriate connection from a known wavegen output to a scope input with shared reference/ground. Configure a low-amplitude 1 kHz sine, arm a short capture, verify its measured frequency and Vpp, then stop the output. Keep the script and connection simple so unexpected measurements are easy to diagnose. For deeper guided experiments, open Signal Lab , AD3 Scope Explorer , Power Supplies , Logic Analyzer , AC Network Laboratory or RC Step Response Laboratory from the bundled examples. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

title: Chapter 8: Digital timing, I/O and protocols
description: Chapter 8 — Digital timing, I/O and protocols The Analog Discovery digital pins make WFScript useful for timing and protocol experiments. The digital services have distinct jobs: StaticIO reads or controls immediate pin state; Patterns1 produces hardware-timed output patterns; Logic1 captures digital samples; and Protocol1 performs supported protocol operations. Static signals
text: Chapter 8 — Digital timing, I/O and protocols The Analog Discovery digital pins make WFScript useful for timing and protocol experiments. The digital services have distinct jobs: StaticIO reads or controls immediate pin state; Patterns1 produces hardware-timed output patterns; Logic1 captures digital samples; and Protocol1 performs supported protocol operations. Static signals are not waveforms A static input monitor can poll pin levels, including optional change callbacks. It is appropriate for button state or relatively slow logic, but its Qt polling interval is not a hardware timestamp. To capture narrow pulses or accurately count fast transitions, use Logic1 hardware-timed sampling. Pattern generation and logic capture Patterns1 can generate digital sequences without requiring JavaScript to toggle pins on every clock edge. The encoder example produces synchronized quadrature A/B/index signals. Logic1 captures 16-bit sample words across the device's digital channels, subject to hardware and configured sampling limits. For a basic loopback, connect one Digital Out pin to a compatible Digital In pin through an appropriate resistor or test fixture, select correct voltage thresholds, and capture the generated transitions. Confirm direction, common ground and ownership: two actively driven outputs should not be tied together. Protocol1 versus PC communications Protocol1.UART , Protocol1.SPI , Protocol1.I2C , Protocol1.CAN and Protocol1.SWD operate through the Digilent digital interface. They are not aliases for a Windows serial COM port or a TCP socket. The PC interfaces Serial , TCP and UDP belong to a different native service and have different timing and framing semantics. Interface Typical connection Specific considerations UART via Protocol1 DIO TX/RX and common ground Baud, parity, inversion, framing SPI Clock, MOSI, MISO, chip select Mode, chip select, voltage compatibility I²C SCL/SDA with suitable pull-ups Open-drain electrical behavior and addresses CAN DIO through external CAN transceiver Never connect DIO directly to CAN_H/CAN_L SWD SWCLK, SWDIO and target ground Target voltage and reset requirements The UART Async Lab illustrates a native receive-queue pattern and terminal widget. The Logic Analyzer and Digital Timing Charts examples illustrate timing acquisition. All hardware demonstrations need safe wiring and must distinguish a successful simulated transfer from a physical-device verification. Timeouts, releases and shared pins Protocols and digital output generators may compete for the same device pins. Choose a single owner, reserve pins deliberately, and stop one service before handing pins to another. Protocol calls can return an error or require a stop/release operation; don't leave a pin driven merely because a script reached its last line. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

title: Chapter 9: Serial, TCP and UDP communications
description: Chapter 9 — Serial, TCP and UDP communications WFScript supplies Qt-backed PC communications through native JavaScript objects. You can build a serial terminal, network monitor, Modbus-style application protocol, or a test controller that communicates with external instruments. Network code must still handle framing, partial messages, timeouts and a remote peer disappearing. A
text: Chapter 9 — Serial, TCP and UDP communications WFScript supplies Qt-backed PC communications through native JavaScript objects. You can build a serial terminal, network monitor, Modbus-style application protocol, or a test controller that communicates with external instruments. Network code must still handle framing, partial messages, timeouts and a remote peer disappearing. A communication session belongs to its owner Create a connection from the Panel's long-lived script, register event handlers, and close it when the Panel stops. Avoid starting a new socket every time an operator presses a measurement button. Multiple requests that share one SCPI instrument should be serialized; the Rigol WFScpiCore library already implements that discipline for its instruments. Serial ports Serial.ports() lists the PC's available serial ports. Serial.create({...}) creates a connection object; register appropriate events such as line/data or binary, then open the port. USB-to-serial cabling, baud rate and RX/TX loopback are separate concerns from AD3 Protocol UART. TCP client and server var client = TCP.create({host:'127.0.0.1',port:5025}); client.on('data', function(bytes) { // Parse the received bytes according to your protocol. }); client.on('error', function(message) { print('TCP error: ' + String(message)); }); Localhost is useful for a simulation-free transport test. Replace the endpoint with a real device only when you have verified the network address and the device-specific protocol. TCP is a byte stream, not a record protocol: one send may arrive as several chunks, and several sends may arrive together. UDP datagrams Use UDP.create() to bind or send datagrams. Unlike TCP, message boundaries are preserved, but UDP has no built-in delivery or ordering guarantee. If a measurement application requires confirmation, sequence numbers or retries, build them explicitly into the application protocol. Binary receives and performance For large binary transfers, use the opt-in binary / binaryMessage event paths that supply native buffers where supported. Keep work in bulk native operations when possible. Many tiny script-to-native reads can be slower than a JavaScript loop, while a single native parse or aggregation over a large buffer can be much faster. External SCPI on a real test bench SCPI text commands are human-readable, but real instruments still have model-specific restrictions and binary framing rules. A good wrapper owns one queue per device, has bounded timeouts, reads device errors deliberately, and separates read-only queries from changes that could energize an output. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 10 — Files, SQLite and native binary data Data becomes more valuable when it can be saved, reloaded and compared. WFScript supports restricted file operations, CSV/JSON utilities, SQLite databases and native binary buffers. Choose the simplest representation that preserves your measurement meaning. FileIO: small, readable files Use JSON for configuration, CSV for measurements and portable tables, and native bytes when structured binary records matter. The FileIO API uses allowed PanelData paths or explicit user-granted paths instead of unconstrained filesystem access. var path = FileIO.dataPath('station-settings.json'); FileIO.writeJson(path, {testName:'Power Check',limits:{low:3.2,high:3.4}}); var saved = FileIO.readJson(path); Treat file-access failures as expected application events: missing folders, invalid names, permissions and malformed JSON should produce helpful operator messages rather than silently resetting settings. SQLite: structured and persistent records Database uses asynchronous Qt SQL work. Database.open() creates or opens a named database, Database.exec() executes prepared parameterized statements and Database.query() returns columns and rows. Success is indicated by a callback result with ok:true ; the positive request ID merely indicates the operation was accepted for processing. Database.open('measurements.db', function(opened) { if (!opened.ok) return print(opened.error); var db = opened.db; Database.exec(db, 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS readings (time TEXT, volts REAL)', [], function(created) { if (!created.ok) return print(created.error); Database.exec(db, 'INSERT INTO readings(time,volts) VALUES (?,?)', [new Date().toISOString(), 3.301], function(written) { if (!written.ok) print(written.error); }); }); }); SQL NULL is not the same as an empty string or zero. RC1.5.14.10.8 specifically corrected SQL NULL readback into JavaScript null , and its native regression test now passes. Query results should be validated before publishing them into tables or limit calculations. Binary: keep high-volume work near the data The Binary service creates native buffers and supports integer/floating-point reads, checksums, packing, IEEE 488.2 framing, streams and decoded sample containers. Use it when a task naturally handles many kilobytes or large sample arrays; ordinary form values are simpler as JavaScript Numbers and strings. Avoid calling a native scalar accessor once per element when you can decode a whole series in one operation. The performance lab demonstrated why the JavaScript/native crossing matters: bulk processing scales well, but per-field calls may not. The difference between report data and raw data Test Executive reports should store compact measurements, verdicts, units, run metadata and meaningful references. A 100,000-sample waveform is better handled by a bounded binary/file path. Don't feed a huge raw array into every step completion event merely because JSON supports arrays. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

title: Chapter 11: The native Test Executive
description: Chapter 11 — The native Test Executive The native Test Executive is designed to make sequences editable, reproducible and reportable without requiring every developer to invent a scheduling engine. The Visual Test Sequence Editor stores a project-owned definition: step order, groups, parameters, limits, callbacks, repeat/sweep rules, conditions and report policy. Three logical
text: Chapter 11 — The native Test Executive The native Test Executive is designed to make sequences editable, reproducible and reportable without requiring every developer to invent a scheduling engine. The Visual Test Sequence Editor stores a project-owned definition: step order, groups, parameters, limits, callbacks, repeat/sweep rules, conditions and report policy. Three logical groups Setup establishes readiness and prepares a known state. Main performs measurements and controlled actions. Cleanup attempts to release equipment and record final state regardless of the normal path through Main. The Cleanup group is essential for test stations, though software alone cannot guarantee physical outputs OFF after a disconnected instrument. A test definition can contain action steps, numeric tests, grouped loops and branches. Numeric acceptance is evaluated by the native Test Executive, not by repeated ad-hoc JavaScript comparison code inside each instrument handler. The operator script stays small The Panel's main script typically shows status, starts or stops the TestRunner, handles operator inputs, and updates a few high-level displays. Reusable test procedures live in the project-owned .mjs Test Library. The visual editor selects those exported handlers by name. This is substantially clearer than reconstructing a hidden test sequence with TestRunner.configure() calls at startup. The project definition is the source of truth and can be inspected without following a maze of dynamic script setup functions. Step configuration For each step, choose an ID, display name, group, mode, optional handler, parameters, deadline and relevant acceptance rules. A numeric test may return a finite number, or a structured object with multiple named numeric paths. Named Results & Limits in the editor determine which paths must pass. A callback handler receives a step context: // An embedded Test Library handler, not a built-in global function. export function verifyVoltage(step) { var expected = Number(step.params.targetVoltage); // Start an asynchronous instrument operation here. // On completion, check TestRunner.isActive(step.token), // then call TestRunner.complete(step.token, measuredVoltage). } The comment is intentional: physical output methods differ by driver and should not be invented in a generic example. Use the named real instrument API in your actual test library. Returning structured results TestRunner.complete(step.token, { sourceVoltage: 5.000, meterVoltage: 4.997, errorMilliVolts: 3.0 }); The native definition can attach separate lower/upper bounds to each named result path, determine PASS/FAIL, and write the measurements to the report. The returned object is not a substitute for explicit limit definitions. When to use immediate, poll or callback modes Once is appropriate for a result available immediately. Poll fits cooperative status checks that return progress over time. Callback is appropriate for delayed I/O and Promise chains; the handler schedules work and finishes only by calling TestRunner.complete() or TestRunner.fail() with the current token. The executive does not automatically await a returned JavaScript Promise. Stop and abort are not equivalent Normal test termination requests cooperative Cleanup. Emergency abort may skip sequence-level Cleanup. A pending external SCPI command can complete after a test token expires; stale callbacks must be rejected, and instrument wrappers must not silently issue more commands for a canceled step. The operator must still verify physical output state after faults. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

title: Chapter 12: Sweeps, loops and conditional execution
description: Chapter 12 — Sweeps, loops and conditional execution The most useful test sequences are declarative. Instead of copying a step for every voltage or frequency, define the parameters that change and reuse one procedure. The native engine expands the authored sequence into executable steps before the run, assigns each a unique token, evaluates limits independently and produces a s
text: Chapter 12 — Sweeps, loops and conditional execution The most useful test sequences are declarative. Instead of copying a step for every voltage or frequency, define the parameters that change and reuse one procedure. The native engine expands the authored sequence into executable steps before the run, assigns each a unique token, evaluates limits independently and produces a separate report row. One voltage sweep, many measurements A supply verification might test 2, 3, 4 and 5 V. The authored sweep contains an axis named voltage ; its child procedure reads step.params.voltage , configures the instrument under the test policy, waits for settling, measures the result, and returns structured values. The visual definition, not the procedure code, owns lower and upper acceptance limits. A numeric sweep may use a start/stop/increment range. A list sweep can enumerate discrete choices, such as sine/square shape. Multiple axes produce Cartesian combinations; nested groups produce ordered sub-sequences. Repetition can test repeatability at each condition without manually writing another loop in JavaScript. Limits can follow the sweep point A measurement intended to track the programmed voltage can use relative bounds based on the current voltage parameter. The editor resolves these limits per expanded step so the report records the actual acceptance range. Setpoint Example lower limit Example upper limit 2.0 V 1.9 V 2.1 V 3.0 V 2.9 V 3.1 V 4.0 V 3.9 V 4.1 V 5.0 V 4.9 V 5.1 V These limits illustrate a tolerance; they are not a manufacturer's instrument specification. Configure acceptance to suit the UUT and measurement method. Conditions and nested branches Conditional groups let a sequence select THEN or ELSE work according to named values and a predicate. A nested diagnostic sweep can run only under the failure branch. The visual Execution Preview shows the expanded plan and how grouping affects execution, while actual runtime decisions depend on the values observed during the run. Branch paths not taken are marked SKIPPED , not silently removed from the authored definition. This matters for report traceability: the report should make clear what was tested and what was intentionally bypassed. Preview before committing Use Execution Preview to inspect the expanded step count, parameter combinations and generated IDs. This is especially important before large Cartesian sweeps: two axes of 10 points produce 100 conditions, and adding repeats or child steps multiplies the final workload. The source defines bounded expansion and maximum step counts; the editor validates before execution rather than trying to build an unlimited plan. Keep equipment changes deliberate A sweep across an active supply output is still a series of physical setpoint changes. Validate the safe range, configure protection, and make sure Cleanup can release the channel. A syntactically valid loop is not a substitute for a fixture safety review. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 13 — Operator input and manual steps Not every automated procedure is fully automatic. Some tests require an operator to identify the unit, confirm a fixture, enter a measured dimension or inspect a display. WFScript supports asynchronous operator dialogs through Tool and project-owned Run Information. Run Information describes the test specimen Define UUT identifiers, operator names, work-order fields, choices or other required fields in the Test Sequence Editor. They are displayed as native operator inputs before execution and captured as a run-specific snapshot in reports. Reject missing or invalid required values before energizing equipment. Dialogs are asynchronous Tool.question , Tool.getNumber , Tool.getText and related dialogs invoke a callback after the operator responds; they do not synchronously return the entered value. To use one in a callback Test Executive step, keep the step token and call TestRunner.complete() or fail() only when the response arrives. export function inspectFixture(step) { Tool.question('Is the fixture securely connected?', function(reply) { if (!TestRunner.isActive(step.token)) return; if (!reply.accepted || !reply.value) { TestRunner.fail(step.token, 'Fixture not confirmed'); return; } TestRunner.complete(step.token, true); }); } The example illustrates the callback contract. Confirm the exact return object and supported dialog variants in the API Reference before making a production procedure; the Test Executive itself doesn't supply a safety-rated hardware interlock. Entered measurement versus commanded value If an operator supplies a measured number, return that number or a structured object to the native limit evaluator. Do not quietly convert an unanswered dialog into zero or PASS. Include the source of the measurement (manual, instrument or computed) in its description or metadata when it matters to acceptance. Operator cancellation and cleanup A canceled manual dialog should fail or terminate the relevant step explicitly. The native executive will follow its stop/error policy; use Cleanup for any equipment that the run may have energized. A remote instrument command already sent before a dialog is shown is not canceled merely because the dialog disappears. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

title: Chapter 14: Reports, measurements and history
description: Chapter 14 — Reports, measurements and history Reports turn a working test script into a reproducible process. A useful run record answers: what was tested, when, by whom, with which procedure, what values were measured, which limits were applied, and how the run finished. Choose the right operator widget The Test Sequence / Progress widget shows step states; Measurement Table
text: Chapter 14 — Reports, measurements and history Reports turn a working test script into a reproducible process. A useful run record answers: what was tested, when, by whom, with which procedure, what values were measured, which limits were applied, and how the run finished. Choose the right operator widget The Test Sequence / Progress widget shows step states; Measurement Table shows individual named measurements and verdicts; Event Log shows execution messages; Measurement Result provides a compact large display. A results-oriented Panel can show a short dashboard without duplicating all native report state in custom JavaScript arrays. Structured results become rows A callback result such as {frequencyHz:999.8, vpp:1.001, shape:0.354} may produce three independent numeric checks. The result object is data; the definition supplies labels, units and limits. Give names to measurements that are stable enough to compare across runs, rather than relying on their position in an array. The Results Browser WFScript can browse archived runs, search metadata, inspect per-step details, and export JSON or CSV. Files created by this native reporting mechanism are distinct from arbitrary FileIO exports. Both can be useful: a formal report captures the verdict, while a separate waveform file can preserve the raw evidence. Data provenance and simulations The Results Browser screenshot includes a field showing simulation . That field is not sufficient proof that every external TCP instrument operation was simulated. When physical SCPI instruments are involved, record their actual *IDN? identities or serial information in run metadata where the application supports it, and verify that the report's mode label isn't inherited from the unrelated native hardware context. Repeatability before convenience Do not change acceptance limits just to obtain a green report. Prefer a reproducible test definition, a meaningful version identifier and an explanation of environmental conditions. When a measured result fails, preserve the failure and its raw or diagnostic evidence instead of silently rerunning until it passes. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

Four embedded JavaScript drivers sit above the shared WFScpiCore.mjs transport: Instrument Driver module Typical purpose Rigol DP932A RigolDP900.mjs Protected DC supply programming a
text: Chapter 15 — External Rigol instruments and SCPI Panels The Rigol example suite demonstrates how WFScript can host an external-instrument application without hard-coding Rigol into its C++ runtime. Four embedded JavaScript drivers sit above the shared WFScpiCore.mjs transport: Instrument Driver module Typical purpose Rigol DP932A RigolDP900.mjs Protected DC supply programming and readback Rigol DM858 RigolDM858.mjs Independent multimeter measurements Rigol DG902 Pro RigolDG900Pro.mjs Function generation, channel readback Rigol MHO954 RigolMHO900.mjs Scope setup, measurements, waveform download The shared core owns command serialization, reply framing, IEEE blocks and timeout handling. The Rigol Test Station v0.7.2 adds a guarded RigolTestApi.mjs facade that exposes focused Promise-returning operations, enforces conservative test-profile limits, and tracks output ownership. Do not bypass those protections inside an executing test by opening a competing SCPI socket. Two applications, two jobs The Operator Bench is an interactive manual instrument workbench. The Automated Test Station is a streamlined, results-first application that runs named procedures under the native Test Executive. The distinction is architectural, not merely a difference in page layout. The v0.7.2 Test Station authors 12 steps, expands to 21 executable steps and expects 39 numeric checks on a successful composite run. Its original DC and sine/square tests are followed by synchronized dual-channel Normal capture and stopped-record RAW acquisition. Those newer two-channel and RAW paths are still awaiting physical validation with the planned BNC splitter setup; offline mocks are not equivalent to a real MHO954 transfer. Instrument connections are not harmless The Panel's SCPI endpoints are configuration, not universal defaults. Before RUN, verify actual IP address and port, identify each instrument, confirm the required physical wiring, and inspect all possible source output states. The source architecture deliberately avoids resetting or energizing outputs merely by connecting. Output ownership, unknown state and cleanup The guarded facade checks output state and remembers which channels the test deliberately changed. Cleanup attempts instrument-reported OFF across owned channels; communication failure makes output state unknown , not automatically safe. Confirm terminal voltage or generator output independently when the consequences matter. Network transport shutdown is not a physical emergency-stop function. Synchronized captures are a real acquisition property Two sequential scope.chN.capture() calls are not simultaneous. A synchronized capture requests selected scope channels from one stopped record with aligned timestamps. The test-facing Rigol.scope.captureMulti() and Rigol.scope.captureRaw() are distinct from the raw MHO954 driver methods and have their own software limits. For the planned dual-channel test, DG902 Pro CH1 feeds both MHO954 CH1 and CH2 through a suitable BNC splitter, with both scope inputs configured for compatible high impedance. The expected splitter reference is approximately 0 dB gain and 0° relative sine phase, subject to wiring and calibration. Keep the DP932A/DM858 voltage path separate and confirm that all five source channels start OFF. What the low-level drivers add The driver catalog exposes far more than the test facade: additional generator functions, acquisition options, protection diagnostics, status registers, instrument files and network configuration. Use those advanced calls only when the application can enforce equivalent safety and serialization rules. The separate Rigol SCPI API Guide documents those methods; they are not native WFScript global APIs. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

text: Chapter 16 — Building complete applications A well-structured Panel is easier to change than a powerful but entangled one. The following structure works well for a multi-page measurement application: Location Owns Example Pages Layout for Controls, Results, Settings and Diagnostics Controls Page Panel Data Cross-Page state and computed values Acquisition.Running Main script Startup, user events and display coordination onCaptureClicked() Signal library Reusable processing spectrum, smoothing, calibration Device/SCPI library Connection, serialization and error handling captureWaveform() Test library Named step procedures and compact return objects verifyChannel() Test definition Execution order, sweeps, limits and report policy Setup/Main/Cleanup One source of truth per value An operator setpoint should not be stored independently as a widget value, a second JavaScript global and another Panel Data variable unless each has a clearly different meaning. Declare the shared state, bind the widget, and let the communication layer consume it through a validated operation. One owner per connection A device driver should own its socket and queue. The UI requests measurements through the driver; it should not send raw SCPI while the driver is in the middle of a framed binary transfer. Keep scope data inside a bulk processing path rather than repeatedly converting samples through GUI updates. Name operations for their purpose Methods such as verifySupplyChannel() or captureAlignedPair() express the intended operation better than a UI handler containing a dozen literal SCPI strings. Keep the lower-level commands accessible in the driver module for diagnostics, but make the common workflow readable. A helpful first screen The Page should explain the required wiring or startup state, show connected/disconnected status, and make the primary next action obvious. If RUN is blocked, explain why . Don't leave the operator to infer that a network timeout means the physical output is OFF. ← Previous chapter Next chapter →

Watch shows declared data changes; it does not inspect arbitrary local QJSEngine variables or support full breakpoint/stack debugging. For complex module execution, add concise, structured diagnostics at the API boundaries. Hardware troubleshooting Check ground, termination, safe input ranges and actual instrument settings before altering software. Start with a slow, low-voltage signal known to be present. A scope trace clipping at its configured range often means the requested scale is inadequate, not that the source voltage is capped there. Avoid hiding errors If a device query fails, keep the failed state visible. A blanket catch that replaces a measurement with zero makes reports look plausible but invalid. The RC1.5.14.10.8 Windows build completed 116/116 native CTests , including Panel lifecycle, widget behavior, charts, communications, Test Executive and SQLite NULL readback. Four different verification levels Source/offline: Python/Node checks and mocks inspect logic and known contracts without compiling Qt. Native CTests: Executables built for Qt 6.9.2 on Windows exercise the real C++ paths and GUI smoke cases. Manual GUI: A developer opens, edits, runs, stops and reopens representative Panels. Physical hardware: Known-safe real instrument tests verify electrical behavior, error recovery, and device state. Record each separately. A passing mock should not be written up as a physically verified signal capture. Before sharing a Panel Test it once with the intended workspace layout, once after save/reopen, once with disconnected devices, and once with a deliberately invalid input. For a test station, also force a failed measurement, canceled dialog, interrupted communication and operator Stop. Confirm that reported outcomes and physical-state warnings remain accurate. Version and change discipline A useful project record identifies the WFScript version, example/Panel version, instrument firmware where relevant, operating system, Qt kit, wiring, report path and test observations. Keep reference documentation compatible with the exact released APIs; an older screenshot is acceptable as an illustration if its version is labelled and no obsolete behavior is presented as current. Solderless breadboard and three short hookup leads (plus AD3 flywires). 1 kΩ resistor (typical 1/4 W) and 100 nF non-polarized ceramic capacitor . The illustrated physical sample has R = 1000 Ω, C = 100 nF, fC ≈ 1591.55 Hz, τ = 100 μs . No AD3 V+/V− power supplies or external powered circuitry are required. Conservative generated sine signal: 0.25–1.00 V peak , 0 V offset , 100 Hz–20 kHz . Do not increase until you understand the circuit and AD3 limits. For physical operation the Panel rejects R below 900 Ω (accepting measured values of nominal 1 kΩ parts, such as 980 Ω). Software R/C values must match installed component values. The software cannot sense resistor/capacitor values or wire placement. Official Digilent AD3 getting-started guide: https://files.digilent.com/manuals/WaveForms/3.24.4/start10.html . text: WFScript AC Laboratory — From physics to JavaScript least-squares measurement Applies to WFScript v0.2-dev.8.9.2. The embedded .wfpanel includes Pages 07 (derivation), 08 (annotated code) and 09 (synthetic / real fit explorer). This companion explanation expands the lessons. The calculation is visible in examples/libraries/CaptureAnalysis.mjs , embedded byte-for-byte in the .wfpanel . 1. Why estimate a sine wave instead of reading one peak? A real Scope records discrete voltages. Even a clean RC filter produces signals with offsets, quantization, interference, harmonic distortion and some noise. A single maximum depends on where the samples land relative to the waveform peak. A zero crossing is similarly sensitive to offsets and noise. Instead, use every sample to estimate the single-frequency sinusoid that best explains the capture. The AD3 generates a nominal sine at a commanded frequency f . The existing acquireOne(f) in ACNetworkLaboratory.js captures both channels during one Scope acquisition and reads back the actual Scope sampling rate as actualRate . The fitting routine treats f as known: it does not independently measure the generator frequency . It also assumes one sample time base for both channels. We fit CH1 and CH2 separately, so each can have an independent offset, amplitude and phase. For sample index i , t_i=i/f_s and θ_i=2π f i/f_s . Write [ y_i=d+a\sin\theta_i+b\cos\theta_i+e_i. ] Unknowns: d = DC offset (V), a = sine coefficient (V), b = cosine coefficient (V), e_i = residual (V). This is linear in the three unknown coefficients even though the waveform is periodic in time. There is no iterative nonlinear optimizer and no need to detect an integer number of periods. 2. Why do sine and cosine encode phase? Using the angle-addition identity, [ A\sin(\theta+\phi)=A\cos\phi\sin\theta+A\sin\phi\cos\theta. ] Therefore a = A cos φ and b = A sin φ ; after fitting, [ \boxed{A=\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\quad \phi=\operatorname{atan2}(b,a)}. ] Warning about argument order: our model is sine plus cosine , so the phase is atan2(cosCoef,sinCoef) . This is a frequent source of mistakes. atan2 also handles the correct quadrant, unlike a plain atan quotient. A nonzero d changes neither A nor φ in the correctly fitted model. 3. Deriving least squares Define s_i = sin θ_i , c_i = cos θ_i , and prediction ŷ_i=d+a s_i+b c_i . Minimize the sum of squared errors: [ S(d,a,b)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(y_i-d-a s_i-b c_i)^2. ] The optimal coefficients satisfy ∂S/∂d = ∂S/∂a = ∂S/∂b = 0 . These three equations are equivalent to the normal equations [ \begin{bmatrix} N&\sum s_i&\sum c_i\ \sum s_i&\sum s_i^2&\sum s_i c_i\ \sum c_i&\sum s_i c_i&\sum c_i^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}d\a\b\end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix}\sum y_i\\sum s_i y_i\\sum c_i y_i\end{bmatrix}. ] This is a linear-algebra problem: the three columns [1,s,c] form a design matrix X . We solve (XᵀX) β = Xᵀy with β=[d,a,b]ᵀ . The 3×3 matrix is never actually allocated; fitSinusoid() only accumulates the necessary sums. 3.1 Eliminate the offset Let s̄ = Σs_i/N , c̄ = Σc_i/N , ȳ = Σy_i/N . Center both basis vectors and the data. Define [ S_{ss}=\sum(s_i-\bar s)^2,\quad S_{sc}=\sum(s_i-\bar s)(c_i-\bar c),\quad S_{cc}=\sum(c_i-\bar c)^2, ] [ S_{sy}=\sum(s_i-\bar s)(y_i-\bar y),\quad S_{cy}=\sum(c_i-\bar c)(y_i-\bar y). ] Then solve only two equations: [ S_{ss}a+S_{sc}b=S_{sy},\qquad S_{sc}a+S_{cc}b=S_{cy}. ] With D=Sss*Scc−Ssc² , [ a=\frac{S_{sy}S_{cc}-S_{cy}S_{sc}}{D},\quad b=\frac{S_{cy}S_{ss}-S_{sy}S_{sc}}{D},\quad d=\bar y-a\bar s-b\bar c. ] This is exactly the technique implemented in the embedded JavaScript. A small D implies that the basis functions cannot be independently resolved for the supplied sample geometry; the code rejects degenerate fits. Normal equations are suitable for this tiny fixed-frequency basis in our bounded captures, but are not a universal numerical method for badly conditioned large least-squares problems. 4. text: Lab 38 — JavaScript DSP Studio: Import, Analyze, Package Level: Intermediate | Category: Graphics & Charts | Pages: One Safety: Simulation only. This example does not use any instrument outputs or sample real hardware. Objective Turn WFScript into a small signal-processing application using reusable JavaScript modules . Compare a clean signal with noise/harmonics, apply a two-pole Butterworth lowpass filter, view the FFT spectrum, and package a complete signal in a portable lossless string. Try it Open Examples → Graphics & Charts → JavaScript DSP Studio — Third-Party Libraries and Run Panel in Simulation. The top chart shows raw and digitally filtered sample values. Change WAVEFORM from Sine to Square or Triangle. Increase 3rd HARMONIC and observe the new spectral peak near three times the tone frequency (subject to Nyquist and sampling). Increase NOISE FLOOR and watch the spectral background rise. Decrease LOWPASS CUTOFF to reduce high-frequency content. The bottom chart shows the predicted magnitude response of the digital biquad , not an analog physical filter. Use NEW NOISE to produce a different seeded noise sequence. Use PACK + VERIFY to test the imported Pako and base64-js modules. Compression and exact round-trip verification run entirely in JavaScript. The Panel reports compressed bytes relative to the original JSON bytes. In Design mode, choose a Button and inspect Properties → Events to open its JavaScript handler; inspect DSPCore.mjs and SignalPackage.mjs in Library Manager. What each third-party library actually does Fraction.js gives a rational samples/cycle ratio ( 16384/440 = 2048/55 exactly), which avoids displaying an approximate frequency-grid ratio as an exact integer. Pako performs actual Deflate compression and decompression on a JSON capture. base64-js converts compressed bytes into text suitable for JSON/transport and back. DSPCore.mjs contains WFScript-authored FFT and filter demonstrations. They are not redistributed FFT.js or Fili and are not certified for metrology. The modules are stored inside the .wfpanel , so the example doesn't require installing Node.js or npm. Explore the package var DSP = modules.load('DSPCore.mjs'); var Package = modules.load('SignalPackage.mjs'); // The Package module itself uses relative ES imports: // import Fraction from './vendor/fraction.mjs'; // import { deflate, inflate } from './vendor/pako.mjs'; // import { fromByteArray, toByteArray } from './vendor/base64.mjs'; The modules.load() return value is a namespace of named exports. The example intentionally avoids manual ui.on() wiring: its Button/input events are stored in the Designer's event properties. Next experiment Replace DSPCore.mjs with a vetted third-party FFT or filter library, preserving the same small interface. Compare numerical outputs and CPU timing against the educational implementation, then repeat using real AD3 samples once a dedicated acquisition adapter has been validated. Full implementation notes: docs/JAVASCRIPT_DSP_STUDIO_V02_DEV8_6.md . Source: examples/guides/JavaScriptDSPStudio.md in RC1.5.14.10.8. text: Lab 37 — Panel Data: Live Workbench Level: Beginner–Intermediate Category: Getting Started Pages: One — Live Workbench Hardware: None. All values are simulated. What you will learn The controls and live readouts are side by side so you can see a data binding respond immediately. The seven project-owned shared variables are named Motor.TargetRPM , Motor.ActualRPM , Motor.LoadPct , Motor.Ready , Motor.Mode , Motor.Status and derived Motor.TargetRPS . These are in-memory runtime values , unrelated to the disk folder named PanelData used by FileIO/SQLite. Follow along Open Examples → Panel Data Lab . In Design mode, open Properties → Panel Data and inspect the six entries. The column is labelled Initial Value because the Panel isn't running. Look at targetInput , loadSlider , readySwitch and modeSelector on the left . Each has an optional Properties → Value Binding . The right-hand targetReadout , loadMeter , and readyBeacon use the same variables. Select speedDisplay , speedDial , and speedGauge on the right . All three bind to Motor.ActualRPM . The targetReadout display instead binds to the computed Motor.TargetRPS variable. No separate JavaScript widget assignments are needed. Before running, find Data.computed('Motor.TargetRPS', ['Motor.TargetRPM'], ...) near the beginning of the script. This formula divides Target RPM by 60, converts it to revolutions per second and updates the targetReadout display automatically. Click Run Panel . The LIVE RESULTS subtitle immediately displays the initial target from Data.onChange(...,{immediate:true}) . Enable READY , adjust Target RPM , and press START SIMULATION . Watch the three speed displays change together without switching Pages . The slower first-order response gives you time to observe the effect. While running, reopen the Properties pane (automatic Focus hides it) and select Panel Data . The third column reads Live Value ; values follow changes, including variables you create yourself before running. While the simulated motor runs, turn READY OFF . A Data.onChange('Motor.Ready',...) subscriber safely stops the simulation without requiring a separate Button event. Re-enable READY and START if desired. Click STOP to stop the model timer, then RESET ALL to restore the simulated values. Click Stop / Design on the toolbar to exit the Panel runtime. The Panel Data column changes back to Initial Value , because runtime values are not saved as defaults. Follow the JavaScript The source is at examples/source/PanelDataLab.js and is embedded in the .wfpanel project. The model runs every 250 ms and publishes one measured speed value: const previous = Data.get('Motor.ActualRPM'); const target = Data.get('Motor.TargetRPM'); const load = Data.get('Motor.LoadPct'); const achievable = target * (1 - 0.0012 * load); Data.set('Motor.ActualRPM', Number((previous + 0.12 * (achievable - previous)).toFixed(1))); All three right-hand speed widgets follow that one Data.set() call. Data.get() reads a variable; Data.names() lists all definitions. Data.isComputed(name) reports whether a definition was registered as a derived read-only value in the current run. Input controls publish changes through their two-way bindings before the saved JavaScript event handler executes. Observe changes without manually wiring widget events The example now registers two Data subscriptions in JavaScript: const targetWatcher = Data.onChange('Motor.TargetRPM', function(value, previous, name) { ui.set('hintControls', 'TARGET ' + value + ' RPM'); }, {immediate:true}); const readyWatcher = Data.onChange('Motor.Ready', function(ready) { if (!ready && modelTimer !== null) stopMotorSimulation(); }); Data.onChange() receives (value, previousValue, name) and returns a numeric subscription ID. The target subscriber executes when you change the targetInput control or when RESET runs Data.set('Motor.TargetRPM',1200) . The READY subscriber stops the simulation when READY is switched off. Modes: SYNTHETIC MODEL (does not touch hardware) and deliberately armed PHYSICAL AD3 (real two-channel Scope samples). Prerequisite: A working WFScript Qt 6 application with the WaveForms SDK and native Panel JavaScript APIs; a physical Digilent Analog Discovery 3 is optional until Page 04. Important: The generated model and the physical sample records are never substituted for each other. The panel is an educational exercise, not an independently calibrated instrument. Learning outcomes By completing this lab, students should be able to: Derive a first-order RC differential equation from KVL and the constitutive equations for a resistor and capacitor. Solve the equation for an arbitrary initial capacitor voltage following a piecewise-constant input change. Relate exponential charging and discharging to the definition of the time constant, including the 63.2% criterion and 5τ settling rule. Predict the steady periodic response to a symmetric square wave without treating each half-cycle as starting from zero volts. Use a physical AD3 to capture both the input step and capacitor response, locate each input edge, and isolate complete transient intervals. Fit an exponential by least squares without a hidden numerical library, learn why the optimization is partly linear and partly nonlinear, and interpret its residuals. Compare rising and falling edge time constants and understand what differences can reveal about noise, component behavior and measurement technique. Determine a cutoff frequency from a time-domain experiment , then connect it to the frequency-domain AC Network Laboratory. Preserve an evidence trail that distinguishes entered component values, synthetic calculations, and actual acquired voltages. Equipment, baseline components and circuit Digilent Analog Discovery 3 (optional for simulation), WaveForms SDK, WFScript v0.2-dev.8.9.2 or a compatible version that supports the existing instrument/visual/widget APIs. One non-polarized capacitor and one resistor, breadboard, AD3 flywires; an optional DMM/LCR meter. The actual components previously measured: R = 980 Ω , C = 571 nF at 1 kHz . These are entered parameters, not measurements made by this project. Electrical connections: W1 to VIN; R from VIN to VCAP; C from VCAP to common ground; CH1+ to VIN; CH2+ to VCAP; W1 GND, CH1−, CH2− to the same ground. No external power supply and no externally energized circuit. Physically use the low-pass topology (capacitor to ground, output across capacitor). Rewire only with W1 OFF. Its 0.5 V peak default means 1 Vpp square wave, not 0.5 Vpp. CH1 and CH2 are set to the same 5 Vpp Scope range as in the earlier AC example. A wiring-confirmation switch is only a checklist.
